style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Okay, before you practice, here's a quick summary of overlapping groups.
Everything important, one idea at a time.
Two groups make four regions. A only, both, B only, and neither. Every person lands in exactly one of them.
Now be careful. "Music students" means the whole circle. Music only, plus both.
Add the two groups... but the middle is counted twice. So subtract it once. Then add the ones outside.
Forty tourists. Twenty-two plus nineteen, minus nine, is thirty-two. So neither is eight.
Now, range questions. A fact is missing, so the overlap isn't one number.
The biggest it can be? Put the small group inside the big one.
Nine and six? Then it's six. Nothing to calculate.
The smallest it must be? Ask, how far do the groups go over the total?
Nine plus six is fifteen, for eleven students. So four must be in both.
And if the sum doesn't go over the total? Then nobody is forced. The minimum is zero... it's never negative.
With fractions, the whole is one. Three quarters plus a third, minus one... at least a twelfth.
Asked about another region? Find the range of the overlap first.
Big overlap means a small union, and then neither is big. And a big overlap means a small A only.
At least, at most... of what? Ask yourself, to make this small, what must the overlap be?
Now, exact questions. Here one more fact fixes every region. So use the squares method.
One strip, four boxes. The two brackets share the middle box, that's the overlap.
Put in the data, and fill the boxes like a sudoku. Start from any box they give you.
Exactly one? Take both away twice. Because it sits inside each group once.
The same people, with two traits? Draw a table. And if it's percents, plug in a hundred.
Ten percent of the teachers and forty percent of the parents? Don't add them, and don't average them. Fill the table.
"Of the people who wear hats"? Then the hats column is the whole.
Three groups? Count who misses a group. Everyone else must be in all three.
In one line: add the three groups, and subtract the total twice. Twenty-five plus twenty-four plus twenty-two, minus two times thirty... eleven.
And the most in all three? That's the smallest group.
They also tell you what each pair shares? Then the most in all three is the smallest pair overlap.
So, before you start, always ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: "music students" is the whole circle, a negative minimum is really zero, and percents of different groups can't be added.
Okay, now it's your turn. Good luck.
